problem-list.title: Problem list implementation
problem-list.subtitle: Implementing a structured SNOMED CT-based problem list in clinical systems
problem-list.overview: A SNOMED CT-based problem list enables structured condition recording that supports longitudinal care, clinical decision support, cohort queries, and interoperability. Concepts from the Clinical finding and Disorder hierarchies are used, scoped by an Expression Constraint Language (ECL) expression or a curated reference set. This is one of the highest-value and most common SNOMED CT implementation targets.

decisions.question: What constitutes a 'problem' in your clinical context?
decisions.guidance: There is no single definition of a 'problem' - it varies by specialty, care setting, and organisation. Clarify whether the list covers active conditions only, includes resolved history, or captures the full range of health concerns. Treat this as a critical starting point, not a detail to settle later: it determines which SNOMED CT hierarchies and value set bindings the rest of the implementation is built on. This is a clinical governance decision - scope agreed early is hard to reverse once data is being captured.

decisions.question: Will concept selection be open or constrained by a value set?
decisions.guidance: An open and high-level constraint (any descendant of Clinical finding) gives maximum flexibility and granularity, but searching across thousands of concepts demands an efficient search mechanism. Relevance ranking, frequency-based ordering, or context-aware suggestions become essential as the constraint gets broader. A manually curated subset is quick to define and easy for clinicians to accept, but it lacks the granularity of a hierarchical (ECL-bounded) constraint and needs more maintenance as SNOMED CT content evolves. A managed subset is often an easy starting point for this reason, widening over time - or giving way to an ECL-bounded constraint. See the Value Sets playbook for how to define and govern it.

decisions.question: What level of clinical granularity is required?
decisions.guidance: The right granularity is rarely a single choice across a workflow: CDS rules and patient-level analytics need the most specific concept the clinician can confidently assert, while population-level reporting can aggregate upward using subsumption (<<) rather than forcing coarser data entry. Capture at the most specific level available and aggregate for reporting, rather than constraining entry to a coarser grain up front. Agree the required depth with clinicians and informaticists before building search and validation logic.

decisions.question: How will preferred terms be displayed to clinicians?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED CT fully specified names (FSNs) is not intended for direct data entry and display in the clinical user interface. Preferred terms from the appropriate language reference set must should be the default display term for data entry. If your system is multilingual, agree on the language priority order.

decisions.question: What is the architecture of the implementation and how is the problem list integrated into the clinical system?
decisions.guidance: Understand the technical architecture before making value set and terminology service decisions. Key questions: Is the problem list a module within an existing EHR, or a standalone system? Can a FHIR terminology service be integrated directly, or must value sets be loaded statically? Is the system built in-house or a commercial product with constraints on integration? The answers determine which value set delivery approach is feasible and how much of the SNOMED CT infrastructure the implementation team controls.

decisions.question: How will the problem list feed downstream systems?
decisions.guidance: Identify which systems consume problem list data - CDS engines, analytics platforms, ICD-10 reporting, FHIR document exchange. Each has different requirements that will constrain your SNOMED CT implementation choices.

steps.title: Define clinical scope and governance policy
steps.description: Work with clinical and governance leads to agree what constitutes a 'problem', who approves changes to the scope, and how the list will be maintained over time.

steps.title: Define the problem list value set
steps.description: Define the concept scope using an ECL expression (e.g. <<404684003 for all clinical findings, or a narrower constraint) or a curated subset. ECL is preferred - it automatically includes new concepts added in each SNOMED CT release. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and testing guidance.

steps.title: Choose how the value set will be delivered
steps.description: Decide whether a FHIR terminology service will be integrated directly into the clinical system (best practice) or whether the value set will be exported as a static concept list. Direct integration keeps concept and term data current with each SNOMED CT release; static exports must be refreshed manually. See the Value set playbook for delivery patterns and trade-offs.

steps.title: Package the value set for the clinical system
steps.description: A raw list of concept IDs is not sufficient - the clinical system needs terms and a structured format. With an integrated terminology service, define a FHIR ValueSet with an ECL compose expression; preferred terms are resolved at runtime. Without one, export the expanded concept list with preferred terms and package as a FHIR ValueSet, RF2 reference set, or CSV. Static representations must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release. See the Value set playbook for packaging options.

steps.title: Implement clinician-facing search
steps.description: Configure search to display preferred terms from the language reference set - never FSNs. Apply the ECL constraint as a search filter on the terminology service API. Default ranking rarely surfaces the most clinically relevant result first - frequency-based and preferred-term boosting need to be layered on top. See the Search and data entry playbook for ranking, synonym configuration, and no-match handling.

steps.title: Establish governance and release management
steps.description: Define who reviews the value set on each SNOMED CT release, how inactivated concepts are handled in existing patient data, and how clinicians can request new concepts or additions to the value set.

dependencies.text: SNOMED CT terminology service - either integrated into the clinical system (best practice) or used separately to extract and export value sets
ECL-defined clinical finding value set or reference set
Clinical and terminology governance framework
Language reference set configured for preferred term display

pitfalls: Displaying FSNs (fully specified names) instead of preferred terms from a language reference set - FSNs are not for clinical display
Using an open constraint (all of SNOMED CT) without scoping - this produces irrelevant search results and poor data quality
Failing to configure the correct national edition in the terminology service, causing local concepts to be missing
Skipping release management - inactivated concepts silently remain in patient records after SNOMED CT updates
Using a static value set extracted from a terminology server without a refresh process - new clinically relevant concepts added in SNOMED CT releases are silently excluded from selection

clin-docs.title: Structured clinical documentation
clin-docs.subtitle: Capturing structured clinical data using SNOMED CT in templates and forms
clin-docs.overview: Structured clinical documentation using SNOMED CT supplements - and sometimes replaces - free text with computable, queryable data. Data entry fields are bound to SNOMED CT value sets, giving clinicians access to clinically appropriate concepts at the point of care. SNOMED International and national release centres publish domain-specific implementation guides that define patterns for recording specific types of clinical information, such as allergies and adverse reactions. The key challenge is balancing clinical expressiveness with usability: over-structuring creates friction, while under-structuring produces data that cannot be queried or exchanged.

decisions.question: Which clinical data elements need to be SNOMED CT coded, and which can remain as narrative?
decisions.guidance: Not every field should be coded. Focus SNOMED CT binding on data that will be queried, exchanged, or used for decision support. Mandatory structured fields with poor UX lead to workarounds - start with the highest-value fields and expand progressively.

decisions.question: How will clinical meaning and context be represented for each structured element?
decisions.guidance: Consider not just what value to capture, but what it means in context. A finding field may need to distinguish between a confirmed finding, a suspected finding, a family history, or an excluded condition. The Context Representation Implementation Guide defines patterns for capturing such meaning. These decisions affect template design, value set scope, and what downstream queries can reliably answer.

decisions.question: What are the value set binding principles for each structured field?
decisions.guidance: Value set binding defines the permissible SNOMED CT concepts for a field. Approaches include ECL-based hierarchy constraints, curated reference sets, and combinations. ECL is a powerful tool for hierarchy-based constraints but not the only approach - some fields are better served by curated lists or reference sets where clinical judgement over individual concepts is required. The binding approach should match the clinical purpose and be maintainable over time. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and governance guidance.

decisions.question: Are there logic rules or dependencies between data elements that need to be established?
decisions.guidance: Some documentation fields are clinically interdependent - for example, a severity field may only be relevant if a finding is confirmed, or a causative agent field may constrain which reaction types are appropriate. Identify and model these dependencies explicitly so that templates can guide clinicians and validate data at entry, rather than relying on post-hoc correction.

decisions.question: What language reference set and display terms will be used for each clinical context?
decisions.guidance: Configure the terminology service to return preferred terms from the appropriate national language reference set. Terms displayed in templates must come from the language reference set - not FSNs or arbitrary synonyms. In multilingual deployments, agree language priority order and fallback behaviour explicitly. See the Search and data entry playbook for term display and synonym configuration guidance.

decisions.question: How will ongoing maintenance, quality assurance, and change management be handled?
decisions.guidance: Structured documentation must remain maintainable as clinical requirements evolve and SNOMED CT is updated. Establish processes that allow value sets and templates to be updated in response to both clinician requests and terminology releases - without requiring full system redevelopment. Track free-text rates, out-of-scope concept usage, and template completion as quality indicators. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

steps.title: Define documentation requirements per clinical area
steps.description: Work with clinical leads to identify which fields require structured SNOMED CT coding, what granularity is needed, and how data will be used downstream. Prioritise fields that feed decision support, analytics, or cross-system exchange - these deliver the most value from structured coding.

steps.title: Determine context representation requirements
steps.description: For each structured field, decide whether clinical context needs to be captured alongside the coded value - for example, whether a finding is confirmed, suspected, or excluded. Consult the Context Representation Implementation Guide to identify the appropriate pattern. These decisions must be made before value set binding, as they affect which concepts are appropriate for each field and how downstream queries should be written.

steps.title: Define value set binding for each structured field
steps.description: Select the appropriate binding approach for each field. ECL is well-suited to hierarchy-based constraints that stay current with new SNOMED CT releases; curated reference sets suit fields where clinical judgement over individual concept inclusion is required. Package value sets as FHIR ValueSet resources for runtime use by the terminology service. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and testing guidance.

steps.title: Establish logic and dependencies between data elements
steps.description: Identify fields that are clinically interdependent and implement the necessary logic in the template or data entry layer - conditional field display, cross-field validation, or guided value selection. Document these dependencies explicitly so they can be maintained as templates evolve.

steps.title: Implement data entry UX with correct term display and validation
steps.description: Build autocomplete and pick-list controls that query the terminology service and display preferred terms from the configured language reference set. Never surface FSNs in clinical-facing UI. Use $validate-code to confirm that a concept submitted by a client is active, from the correct edition, and within the field's value set. See the Search and data entry playbook for ranking, synonym configuration, and no-match handling.

steps.title: Establish maintenance, QA, and change management processes
steps.description: Define processes for updating value sets and templates in response to clinician requests and SNOMED CT releases. Ensure that changes can be made without full system redevelopment. Track quality indicators - free-text rates, out-of-scope concept usage, template completion - and establish governance for who approves changes and how updates are communicated to clinical teams. See the Governance playbook for release review process guidance.

dependencies.text: Terminology service supporting value set expansion ($expand) and code validation ($validate-code)
Value sets defined per documentation field, using ECL constraints or curated reference sets
Language reference set for preferred term display and synonym search
Clinical governance for field binding, context representation, and change management

pitfalls: Replacing free text entirely where supplementing it would be more appropriate - over-structuring creates clinician friction and workarounds
Not considering context representation - a coded value without context (confirmed vs. suspected, patient vs. family history) cannot be reliably queried or exchanged
Defaulting to ECL for all value set bindings - some fields are better served by curated reference sets where clinical judgement over individual concept inclusion is required
Displaying FSNs to clinicians in documentation templates - FSNs are technical identifiers, not display labels
Skipping $validate-code on received or submitted concept IDs - invalid or out-of-scope codes silently enter the clinical record
No change management process - structured documentation becomes a maintenance burden when clinician requirements evolve or SNOMED CT releases inactivate concepts used in existing records

cds.title: Clinical decision support
cds.subtitle: Using SNOMED CT hierarchies and ECL to power computable clinical rules
cds.overview: SNOMED CT enables computable clinical logic through its hierarchical concept model and Expression Constraint Language (ECL). Rules built on SNOMED CT subsumption - using ECL expressions such as <<73211009 for all descendants of Diabetes mellitus - automatically cover all clinically relevant child concepts, including those added in future SNOMED CT releases. This makes CDS rules significantly more durable and clinically complete than rules based on explicit flat code lists.

decisions.question: What clinical logic needs to be expressed as computable rules?
decisions.guidance: Document each rule in plain clinical language before attempting SNOMED CT representation. Alerts, reminders, order sets, contraindication checks, and care pathway triggers all have different implementation patterns. Clarify which rules are mandatory vs. advisory, and what evidence base supports them.

decisions.question: Will rule elements use ECL subsumption queries or explicit concept lists?
decisions.guidance: ECL subsumption (e.g., Value set design and management playbook for authoring guidance.

decisions.question: How will SNOMED CT-coded data be queried at runtime?
decisions.guidance: Clarify whether your CDS engine will call the terminology service API at the point of firing (real-time subsumption check) or use pre-expanded concept sets stored locally. Real-time calls via the terminology service are accurate and always reflect the current SNOMED CT release; pre-expanded sets are faster but require refresh on each release. See step 3 for a detailed comparison of both approaches.

decisions.question: What data quality requirements must be met before CDS is reliable?
decisions.guidance: CDS is only as good as the coded data it queries. Clarify the minimum coding completeness, concept specificity, and recency required before CDS rules will produce meaningful results. Poor data quality can trigger false positives and clinician alert fatigue. Consult the Analytics playbook for query patterns that assess data quality before deploying rules.

decisions.question: How will clinical rules be governed, approved, and retired?
decisions.guidance: Establish a clinical rule lifecycle process before go-live. Rules must be approved by clinical leads, tested against real patient data, versioned, and retired when clinical evidence changes. Governance is as important as the technical implementation.

steps.title: Document each rule in plain clinical language
steps.description: Write each rule as a clinical statement - who it applies to, what it checks, and what action it triggers. This is the source of truth that the SNOMED CT representation must faithfully express. Include the clinical evidence base and the intended alert or action so that both clinical and technical reviewers can validate the final implementation.

steps.title: Map rule elements to SNOMED CT concepts using the Browser
steps.description: Use the SNOMED CT Browser to find the most appropriate concept for each clinical entity in the rule. Prefer finding a single parent concept whose descendants cover all intended cases, enabling a clean ECL subsumption expression. Use the Browser's hierarchy view to verify that the descendant set is clinically appropriate before writing ECL.

steps.title: Write ECL expressions for each rule element
steps.description: Express each rule element as an ECL constraint. Use subsumption (<<) to capture entire disease or drug families. Combine constraints using set operators (AND, OR, MINUS) and attribute refinements for precision. Test expressions using the terminology service $expand operation to confirm the concept set is clinically complete. See the Value set playbook for ECL authoring guidance.

steps.title: Package ECL expressions as value sets for the CDS engine
steps.description: Publish each ECL expression as a versioned FHIR ValueSet resource with a canonical URL. The CDS engine references the value set by URL rather than embedding an inline ECL string, giving rules a stable, auditable concept set that can be updated independently. See the Value set playbook for packaging and versioning patterns.

steps.title: Implement subsumption-based queries via the terminology service
steps.description: Configure the CDS engine to check whether a patient's coded data falls within a rule's SNOMED CT constraint. Use the FHIR $subsumes operation for concept-to-concept hierarchical checks, or $validate-code to confirm a patient concept is within a named value set. This is the standard FHIR Terminology Service pattern. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment and the Analytics playbook for subsumption-based query patterns against clinical data stores.

steps.title: Test, approve, and release each rule through governance
steps.description: Test rules against real patient data, validate results with clinical subject matter experts, and formally approve before go-live. Document the clinical evidence base, the SNOMED CT value sets used (with version), and the planned review schedule. Ensure that historical patient data coded with older SNOMED CT concept IDs is included in testing - inactivated concepts may silently fall outside a rule's value set.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with ECL, $subsumes, and $validate-code support
ECL-defined, versioned value sets for each rule element
Structured, SNOMED CT-coded clinical data of sufficient quality and completeness
Clinical governance process for rule approval, versioning, and retirement

pitfalls: Using explicit concept lists instead of ECL subsumption - new child concepts added in SNOMED CT releases silently fall outside the rule
Firing CDS rules against poorly coded or incomplete data - produces false positives that erode clinician trust
No rule governance - outdated alerts that contradict current evidence persist in production and create clinical risk
Testing only against current SNOMED CT content - historical patient data may use older, now-inactivated concept IDs that fall outside the ECL constraint
Skipping value set versioning - it becomes impossible to audit which concept set a historical rule used when fired
Pre-expanded concept sets without a refresh process - after each SNOMED CT release, new subtypes are silently excluded from rule evaluation

analytics.title: Analytics and reporting
analytics.subtitle: Using SNOMED CT hierarchies and ECL for cohort definition and reporting
analytics.overview: SNOMED CT's hierarchical concept model, queried using Expression Constraint Language (ECL), enables dramatically more powerful cohort queries than flat code matching. ECL expressions using subsumption automatically cover all subtypes of a concept - including types added in future releases - without list maintenance. ECL queries are executed against a terminology service and the resulting concept sets are applied against coded clinical data. If ICD-10 output is required for statutory reporting, see the Mapping playbook for applying the official SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map.

decisions.question: What clinical questions need to be answered from SNOMED CT-coded data?
decisions.guidance: Define the analytic use cases precisely before designing queries - cohort identification, quality indicators, epidemiological surveillance, and operational reporting have different requirements. Clarify the population, time period, data source, and required output before writing ECL.

decisions.question: Will queries use ECL via a live terminology service, or pre-expanded concept sets?
decisions.guidance: ECL via a live terminology service is most accurate and always reflects the current SNOMED CT release. Pre-expanded concept sets (stored in a database or reference set) are faster for high-volume queries but must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release and versioned explicitly. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment and integration options. Choose based on your performance and currency requirements.

decisions.question: How will historical data coded in older SNOMED CT versions be handled?
decisions.guidance: Patient data coded before a SNOMED CT release may use concept IDs that have since been inactivated or split. Use SNOMED CT history supplement reference sets to map historical concept IDs to their current equivalents. Ignoring this produces systematically incomplete cohorts.

decisions.question: Is ICD-10 or other classification output required for external submissions?
decisions.guidance: If SNOMED CT data must be reported as ICD-10, plan for map application early. The official SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map handles the translation via the FHIR $translate operation, but map rules have conditions and priorities that must be applied correctly - it is not a simple lookup. See the Mapping playbook.

decisions.question: How will query results be validated for clinical completeness?
decisions.guidance: Before using ECL queries in production, validate the resulting concept set with clinical SMEs. Check that clinically relevant subtypes are included and that the set boundary is correct. Document validation decisions so queries can be audited. See the Governance playbook for query versioning and review processes.

steps.title: Define the clinical question and cohort precisely
steps.description: Document the clinical question, the target population, the time period, the data source, and the required output. Vague questions produce wrong answers - specificity at this stage prevents expensive rework.

steps.title: Write ECL expressions for each concept group
steps.description: Use subsumption (<<) to capture disease or procedure families. Attribute refinements narrow the expression to a specific clinical meaning - for example, procedures by finding site, or clinical findings by associated morphology. Decide whether queries will run live against the terminology service or use pre-expanded concept sets stored in your data platform.

steps.title: Validate ECL expressions using the terminology service
steps.description: Expand your ECL expressions using the SNOMED CT Browser's ECL search or the FHIR $expand endpoint. Review the resulting concept set with clinical SMEs to confirm it is clinically complete and correctly bounded. Use the count from $expand to sense-check the scope before running against patient data. See the Terminology service playbook for $expand configuration.

steps.title: Handle historical and inactivated concepts
steps.description: Apply SNOMED CT history supplement reference sets to identify historical concept IDs in legacy data and map them to current equivalents. This is essential for any query spanning data collected across multiple SNOMED CT release cycles. Without this step, records coded with now-inactivated concept IDs are silently excluded from cohort results.

steps.title: Build reusable reference sets for repeated queries
steps.description: Package commonly used ECL expressions as named FHIR ValueSet resources or RF2 simple reference sets. This provides a stable, versioned, auditable concept set that analytics queries and reports can reference by name rather than embedding ECL strings inline. Version each reference set explicitly aligned to the SNOMED CT release used to produce it. See the Governance playbook for versioning and change management processes.

steps.title: Apply ICD-10 map for external reporting where required
steps.description: Load the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map in your terminology service as a ConceptMap resource and use the FHIR $translate operation to generate ICD-10 codes for statutory reporting. Apply the full map algorithm including rule groups, priorities, and advice fields - the map is not a simple lookup and incorrect application produces wrong ICD-10 codes. See the Mapping playbook for the full map application process.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with ECL support and FHIR $expand endpoint - see the Terminology service playbook
Clinical data store with SNOMED CT concept IDs persisted at the point of care
Validated ECL expressions or reference sets for each cohort definition

pitfalls: Querying only exact concept IDs - misses all subtypes and equivalent concepts, producing systematically incomplete cohorts
Ignoring history supplements - legacy data coded with inactivated concept IDs is silently excluded from query results
Treating the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map as a simple lookup - map rules have conditions and priorities that must be applied correctly
Not validating ECL expressions with clinical SMEs - the concept set boundary may be incorrect in ways a technical reviewer cannot detect
Pre-expanding concept sets without a refresh process - after a SNOMED CT release, new subtypes are silently excluded
Embedding ECL strings inline in queries without versioning - makes it impossible to audit which concept set was used when a cohort was defined

interop.title: Interoperability and data exchange
interop.subtitle: Exchanging SNOMED CT-coded data between systems using HL7 FHIR
interop.overview: SNOMED CT combined with HL7 FHIR provides a globally interoperable foundation for clinical data exchange. FHIR resources such as Condition, Observation, Procedure, and AllergyIntolerance carry SNOMED CT codes, and FHIR terminology bindings define which value sets (expressed as ECL constraints) are valid for each coded element. A FHIR Terminology Service - implementing operations including $expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, and $translate - is the runtime component that validates, expands, and translates SNOMED CT content. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment guidance.

decisions.question: Which FHIR resources and elements will carry SNOMED CT codes, and with what binding strength?
decisions.guidance: Identify each coded element in your exchange, the FHIR resource and path it maps to, and whether the terminology binding is required, extensible, or preferred. Required bindings enforce conformance; extensible bindings allow extension. The binding strength has significant implications for receiver systems - a required binding means validation failures block processing, while extensible bindings allow locally-defined alternatives.

decisions.question: Which SNOMED CT edition and version will be declared in exchanged resources?
decisions.guidance: Senders must declare the SNOMED CT system URI (http://snomed.info/sct) and, where precision matters, the edition and version (e.g., http://snomed.info/sct/32506021000036107 for the Australian edition). Receivers need this to validate codes correctly. Agree version declaration policy with all exchange partners before go-live.

decisions.question: How will receiving systems validate incoming SNOMED CT codes?
decisions.guidance: Receivers should call $validate-code against their terminology service to confirm that incoming concept IDs are active, valid for the declared SNOMED CT edition/version, and within the expected value set. Accepting codes without validation allows invalid or out-of-scope data into clinical systems.

decisions.question: What display text strategy will be used for different locales?
decisions.guidance: The SNOMED CT display text in a FHIR resource must be the preferred term from the receiver's language reference set - not the sender's preferred term, not the FSN. Call $lookup at the receiver with the target language reference set to obtain the correct display term. Coordinate display text handling with exchange partners, particularly in multilingual or cross-national exchanges.

decisions.question: How will SNOMED CT releases be coordinated across exchange partners?
decisions.guidance: When a sender updates to a new SNOMED CT release before receivers do, concept IDs may temporarily be unresolvable on receiver systems. Agree a release coordination policy - including a transition window - with all exchange partners before upgrading. Ensure all stakeholders have access to the version of SNOMED CT declared in exchanged messages, or have access to a public terminology server that can resolve version mismatches.

decisions.question: What is the resolution strategy when a received concept cannot be validated due to a version or edition mismatch?
decisions.guidance: Two failure modes require different resolution strategies. (1) Concept not found: the sender may be using a newer release or a different national edition - in both cases $validate-code returns 'not found'. Check the national terminology server first for a newer version of the national edition; if still unresolved, query a multi-edition server for the closest international ancestor. (2) Concept inactive: the sender used an older release - apply the proposed replacement from SNOMED CT's historical association reference sets. Define and document these strategies for each exchange partner relationship before go-live.

errorHandling.intro: When $validate-code fails, the response indicates why. Each failure mode has a distinct cause and resolution - do not treat them as equivalent.

scenarios.cause: The sender is using a newer SNOMED CT release or a different national edition. In both cases $validate-code returns 'not found' locally - the detection is the same but the resolution is sequential.
resolutionSteps: Check the relevant national terminology server first - the concept may exist in a newer version of the national edition and resolve to a valid national code.
If still not found, query a shared multi-edition terminology server to find the concept's closest ancestor in the international edition, which is available to both parties.

scenarios.cause: The sender used an older SNOMED CT release. The concept has since been inactivated and a replacement is available in the receiver's version.
resolutionSteps: Look up the inactivated concept in SNOMED CT's historical association reference sets. These identify the proposed replacement concept. Apply that replacement for processing.

errorHandling.note: In all cases, preserve both the original received code and the locally resolved code in the record so the substitution is auditable.

steps.title: Map each exchange element to a FHIR resource, path, and terminology binding
steps.description: Create a data mapping document that identifies every SNOMED CT-coded element, the FHIR resource and element path, the value set (expressed as an ECL constraint or reference set URL), and the binding strength. See the Value set playbook for guidance on defining ECL-based value sets.

steps.title: Define value sets for each terminology binding using ECL
steps.description: Write ECL expressions for each FHIR terminology binding (e.g., <<404684003 for a condition code field). Package these as FHIR ValueSet resources with canonical URLs and an explicit SNOMED CT edition and version in the compose. See the Value set playbook for ECL authoring and packaging guidance.

steps.title: Deploy or configure a FHIR Terminology Service
steps.description: Ensure a FHIR R4-compliant terminology service is available to both sender and receiver systems. It must support $expand with ECL, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, and $translate (for map-based translation via the Mapping playbook). Implementers must deploy or license their own terminology service for production use - the public terminology server operated by SNOMED International is intended for evaluation and testing only, not for production clinical systems. See the Terminology service playbook for full deployment guidance.

steps.title: Implement code validation on receipt
steps.description: On receiving a FHIR resource, call $validate-code for each SNOMED CT-coded element against the declared edition/version and the expected value set. If validation succeeds, the concept is active and within scope - proceed normally. If $validate-code fails, identify the failure mode and apply the corresponding resolution strategy. Define and document these strategies for each exchange partner relationship before go-live.

steps.title: Handle display text using the receiver's language reference set
steps.description: When rendering received SNOMED CT codes, call $lookup against the terminology service with the displayLanguage parameter set to the receiver's language reference set. Display the resulting preferred term - do not use the display text from the received resource as authoritative, as it reflects the sender's locale. Good practice is to preserve the sender's original display text as a secondary label or tooltip so clinicians can see what the sending system recorded - this matters when preferred terms differ significantly across locales for the same concept. When a concept has been resolved via a mismatch strategy, indicate the original received concept to the user if clinically relevant.

steps.title: Test end-to-end with conformance tooling
steps.description: Validate exchanges using FHIR validation tooling and, where applicable, IHE or HL7 connectathon test scripts. Confirm that coded data round-trips correctly - codes sent are correctly validated and displayed at the receiver. Specifically test version and edition mismatch scenarios: send concepts from a newer version and from an older version, and verify the resolution strategies produce the expected outcomes. Use the FHIR Validator (validator.fhir.org) to confirm resource conformance against published profiles.

dependencies.text: FHIR R4-compliant terminology service ($expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, $translate)
FHIR R4 server or integration layer at sender and receiver
Language reference sets configured for each locale involved in exchange
SNOMED CT license for all participating organisations

pitfalls: Sending the FSN as the FHIR display text - receivers will display a technical label to clinicians rather than the appropriate preferred term
Not declaring the SNOMED CT edition and version URI in exchanged resources - receivers cannot validate codes without knowing which edition and version was used
Accepting incoming codes without $validate-code validation - invalid or retired concept IDs silently enter clinical systems

Treating all validation failures as equivalent - a concept from a newer version, an inactivated concept, and a concept from a different edition each require a different resolution strategy; conflating them leads to incorrect handling

No resolution strategy for version mismatches - logging and escalating is not sufficient; receivers must be able to resolve concepts from newer or older versions using a public terminology server and SNOMED CT history supplements

Using extension concepts not available in receiver systems without providing the nearest international ancestor - receivers in a different edition cannot resolve or validate locally created extension concepts
No release coordination policy across exchange partners - a SNOMED CT upgrade on one side causes validation failures on the other without an agreed resolution pathway

value-sets.title: Value set design and management
value-sets.subtitle: Designing, authoring, and maintaining SNOMED CT value sets using ECL and reference sets
value-sets.overview: A value set is a uniquely identifiable set of valid concept identifiers selected from one or more code systems for use in a specific context. In SNOMED CT, value sets define which concepts are valid for a given data element such as a problem list, a diagnosis field, or a procedure picker. The recommended approach is to define value sets intensionally using Expression Constraint Language (ECL): an expression that captures the intended concept scope from the SNOMED CT hierarchy. ECL-based definitions are self-maintaining: new concepts that satisfy the constraint are automatically included on each release and can be evaluated at runtime against any SNOMED CT edition by a terminology service. Where ECL cannot fully capture the intended scope, explicit concept lists (extensional definitions) may be used, but require manual review on every SNOMED CT release.

decisions.question: What is the clinical purpose and context of this value set?
decisions.guidance: Before defining any constraints, document exactly what the value set is for, who will use it, in which system or workflow, and what the consequences of including or excluding borderline concepts are. This clinical specification is the basis for all subsequent design decisions and is required before governance sign-off.

decisions.question: Should the value set be defined intensionally (ECL) or extensionally (explicit list)?
decisions.guidance: Intensional ECL definitions are strongly preferred: they are self-maintaining, adapt to new SNOMED CT content, and are declarative. Explicit lists are appropriate only for small, highly curated sets where clinical judgement over individual concepts is required, or where the content cannot be expressed by ECL alone.

decisions.question: What SNOMED CT hierarchy, attribute constraint, or reference set membership best captures the clinical scope?
decisions.guidance: Explore the SNOMED CT Browser to find the most specific ancestor concept that covers the intended content. Consider whether attribute refinement (e.g. finding site, causative agent) is needed for precision. Check whether an existing reference set or FHIR ValueSet already covers your need before authoring a new one.

decisions.question: How will the value set be delivered to and consumed by clinical systems?
decisions.guidance: Integrating a FHIR terminology service is best practice: it enables live ECL expansion, preferred term retrieval, and concept search at runtime. Where direct integration is not feasible, the value set must be exported as a static representation (FHIR ValueSet with explicit entries, CSV, or RF2 reference set) and refreshed on each SNOMED CT release. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment options.

decisions.question: How should the value set be packaged and distributed: RF2 reference set or FHIR ValueSet?
decisions.guidance: RF2 simple reference sets are the native SNOMED CT format and are supported by terminology servers and RF2-aware authoring tools. FHIR ValueSet resources are required for FHIR-based systems and support ECL via the compose.include.filter. Agree the packaging format with consuming systems before authoring.

decisions.question: Who has clinical authority to approve content, and what is the review cadence?
decisions.guidance: Every value set requires a named clinical owner who approves the initial content and reviews it on each SNOMED CT release. Define the governance process, approval workflow, and minimum review frequency before the value set is used in production.

steps.title: Define the clinical purpose and scope
steps.description: Document exactly what the value set is for, who will use it, in what clinical context, and what the consequences of including or excluding borderline concepts are. This clinical specification is the basis for all subsequent design decisions and must be agreed with clinical and governance leads before authoring begins.

steps.title: Explore the SNOMED CT hierarchy and define the concept scope
steps.description: Use the SNOMED CT Browser to navigate the hierarchy and identify the most appropriate ancestor concept and any necessary attribute refinements. Review whether existing reference sets or value sets already meet your need before creating a new one. Two definition approaches are available - choose based on whether clinical intent can be fully expressed as an ECL expression.

steps.title: Write and test the ECL expression
steps.description: Write an ECL expression using subsumption (<<), attribute refinements, and set operators as needed. Test the expansion using the Browser's ECL search or the FHIR $expand endpoint against a terminology service. Verify the concept set boundary with clinical SMEs: both false inclusions and missing concepts.

steps.title: Choose how the value set will be delivered
steps.description: Integrating a FHIR terminology service directly into the clinical system is best practice: it enables live ECL expansion, concept search, and preferred term retrieval against the current SNOMED CT release. Where direct integration is not feasible, a separate terminology server can be used to extract and export the concept list. In either case, a raw list of concept IDs is not yet a usable value set. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment and integration guidance.

steps.title: Represent the value set in a form the clinical system can use
steps.description: A list of concept IDs alone is not sufficient: the clinical system needs terms and a structured format it can process. The right approach depends on your architecture.

steps.title: Author and publish with versioning
steps.description: Choose an authoring approach suited to the value set's complexity. For straightforward value sets and reference sets, Simplex (a free tool from SNOMED International) provides a streamlined workflow. For reference sets that need to be released as part of a SNOMED CT edition, the SNOMED Authoring Platform (available to national release centres and members through the Managed Service) supports full classification and validation. Commercial authoring tools also exist. Assign a canonical URI (for FHIR ValueSet) or a SCTID (for RF2 reference sets). Publish with version metadata aligned to the SNOMED CT release cycle, and define a change notification process for all consuming systems.

steps.title: Establish governance and release management
steps.description: Review the value set on each relevant SNOMED CT release: the International Edition is released monthly, and national extensions follow their own release cycle. Check whether new concepts satisfy the ECL constraint and whether inactivated concepts have been handled. Define who reviews the value set, how inactivated concepts are handled in existing data, and how consumers are notified of changes. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with ECL expansion ($expand) support
Named clinical SMEs for scope definition and validation
Governance process for approval, versioning, and change notification

pitfalls: Using extensional (explicit list) definitions where ECL would suffice: lists require manual maintenance on every SNOMED CT release
Using a static value set extracted from a terminology server without a refresh process: new clinically relevant concepts added in SNOMED CT releases are silently excluded
No clinical review: value sets not validated by clinical SMEs may exclude concepts clinicians expect, or include concepts that are inappropriate in context
Publishing without versioning: consuming systems cannot detect changes and continue using stale pre-expanded sets
Not checking whether an existing value set meets the need: duplicating content that is already maintained creates unnecessary ongoing maintenance burden
No governance: value sets with no named clinical owner degrade in quality as the SNOMED CT release evolves

term-service.title: Terminology service implementation
term-service.subtitle: Providing SNOMED CT terminology services to clinical applications, from use cases to deployment and version upgrades
term-service.overview: A SNOMED CT terminology service is the runtime foundation for all SNOMED CT-enabled applications. It provides concept lookup, preferred term retrieval by language reference set, ECL-based value set expansion, subsumption testing, code validation, and concept map translation. The standard interface is the HL7 FHIR Terminology Service, which defines operations including $expand, $lookup, $subsumes, $validate-code, and $translate. Multiple server implementations are available: Snowstorm (open source, developed by SNOMED International) is widely used, and commercial and hosted options also exist. All other playbooks on this site depend on a correctly configured terminology service.

decisions.question: Will you host your own terminology service or use a hosted or public service?
decisions.guidance: Self-hosting an open-source server such as Snowstorm (from SNOMED International) gives full control over editions, versions, extension content, and language configuration, but requires infrastructure capacity and operational maturity. Commercial and hosted services reduce operational burden but may have latency, edition coverage, or customisation constraints. Some national release centres (NRCs) provide hosted terminology services for their territory. The public SNOMED International terminology server is intended for evaluation and testing only, not for production clinical applications. Assess your uptime, data sovereignty, customisation, and performance requirements before deciding.

decisions.question: Which SNOMED CT edition(s) and language reference sets are required?
decisions.guidance: Most implementations require the national edition, which includes the international release plus national extension content. Check which edition your NRC publishes, whether it includes required local concepts, and the release schedule. If no national edition exists for your territory, load the international edition directly. Configure language reference set priority so that preferred terms are returned in the correct language for your users. See the Multilingual implementation playbook for language reference set configuration guidance.

decisions.question: Which FHIR Terminology Service operations must be supported?
decisions.guidance: At a minimum, most implementations need: $expand (ECL-based value set expansion for search and validation), $lookup (concept details and preferred terms), $validate-code (code validation on receipt), and $subsumes (hierarchical relationship testing for CDS). Translation via $translate is required if ICD-10 or other map output is needed. List the operations required by each consuming system before selecting or configuring a server. See the Interoperability playbook for how these operations are used in FHIR-based data exchange.

decisions.question: How will SNOMED CT release upgrades be tested and deployed?
decisions.guidance: The International Edition is released monthly, and national extensions follow their own release cycle - track both. Upgrades must be tested against all consuming applications before production deployment: value sets may change, concepts may be inactivated, and preferred terms may be updated. Define a testing protocol, rollback procedure, and notification process for consuming systems. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

decisions.question: What access control, audit logging, and availability requirements apply?
decisions.guidance: Clinical applications that depend on the terminology service for validation require high availability. Define SLAs, logging requirements, and access control (especially for write operations) before deployment. Consider caching strategies to reduce load on the terminology service for frequently used concept lookups. Snowstorm supports read replicas and can be deployed behind a load balancer for high-availability configurations.

steps.title: Select deployment model and provision infrastructure
steps.description: Choose between self-hosting an open-source server (such as Snowstorm from SNOMED International), using a hosted service from your NRC or a commercial provider, or using the SNOMED International public terminology server. Self-hosting is required if you need a national edition, extension content, or tight availability SLAs. For development and evaluation, the public SNOMED International server is available but must not be used for production clinical applications.

steps.title: Load the correct SNOMED CT RF2 release content
steps.description: Obtain licensed RF2 release files from SNOMED International (via the MLDS) or your NRC. Load order matters: the international edition must be loaded first, then the national edition on top. Verify content integrity and concept counts after loading. The correct edition determines which concepts are available for search, validation, and expansion.

steps.title: Configure language reference sets for preferred term retrieval
steps.description: Configure language reference set priority in your terminology server so that $lookup, $expand, and concept search operations return preferred terms in the correct language for your users. Most FHIR-compliant servers (including Snowstorm) support language reference set priority ordering: if no preferred term exists in the highest-priority reference set for a concept, the server falls through to the next. Set a fallback reference set for concepts not covered by the primary one. Test explicitly that FSNs are not returned as display terms in any operation. See the Search and data entry playbook for how language configuration affects clinician-facing search.

steps.title: Expose and test FHIR Terminology Service endpoints
steps.description: Enable the FHIR R4 Terminology Service endpoints. Test each operation with realistic SNOMED CT content: $expand with ECL expressions, $validate-code for both valid and invalid concepts, $subsumes for parent-child relationships, and $translate for map-based operations. Confirm that preferred terms are returned correctly in all responses. Use the FHIR Validator or the SNOMED International test harness for conformance testing.

steps.title: Integrate with clinical applications
steps.description: Provide the FHIR Terminology Service base URL to consuming applications. For each consuming system, document which operations are used, the ECL constraints applied per field, and the language reference set configured. Implement a caching layer for high-frequency lookups where appropriate. See the Value set design and management playbook for how consuming systems should define and reference value sets, and the Interoperability playbook for FHIR exchange patterns that depend on the terminology service.

steps.title: Implement and test the release upgrade pipeline
steps.description: Create a documented pipeline to load new SNOMED CT releases into a staging environment, run regression tests against consuming applications, and promote to production. Test the full upgrade procedure before it is needed in production. Document the rollback procedure and the notification process for consuming systems. Align the upgrade schedule with the release cycles of both the international edition and the national edition. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

dependencies.text: SNOMED CT license and access to release packages (via MLDS or your NRC)
The editions, versions, and language reference sets each consuming system needs
A SNOMED CT-enabled terminology server, or application components that implement the required service types
Technical staff to run the service and terminology staff to manage editions, languages, and upgrades
Access control, audit logging, and availability arrangements for production use

pitfalls: Loading only the international edition when a national edition exists for your territory - local concepts, national reference sets, and national language reference sets are absent from search and validation results

Not configuring language reference set priority in the terminology server - the server returns FSNs or wrong-language preferred terms to clinical applications when no language reference set is configured

Using a public or shared terminology server in production - public servers (including the SNOMED International public server) are intended for development and testing and do not carry the SLA required for clinical use
No release upgrade testing pipeline - a SNOMED CT release may inactivate concepts or update preferred terms in ways that silently break consuming applications
No caching strategy for high-frequency lookups - clinical applications experience latency or timeouts under realistic load without a caching layer
Allowing clinical applications to maintain their own local concept caches without a refresh process - cached content diverges from the terminology service after each SNOMED CT release

search-ux.title: Search and data entry
search-ux.subtitle: Designing clinician-friendly SNOMED CT concept search and data entry experiences
search-ux.overview: Search is the primary interface between clinicians and SNOMED CT. The SNOMED CT Search and Data Entry Guide sets out the core principles: scope every field to a clinically appropriate concept space, return only preferred terms from the language reference set (never FSNs), rank results the way clinicians actually read them, and give users a deliberate route when no concept matches. A FHIR-compliant terminology service is the standard runtime for these capabilities. The same principles apply on any terminology service or custom search database; if you use a platform other than a maintained SNOMED CT terminology server, verify that ECL-equivalent scoping, language reference set-based term display, full-text ranking, and active-concept filtering are each actually enabled.

decisions.question: What is the intended concept search scope for each data entry field?
decisions.guidance: Each field must be bound to a specific concept space - typically an ECL constraint (for example a diagnosis field might be scoped to descendants of Clinical finding, while a procedure field is scoped to descendants of Procedure). Binding at the ECL level lets the terminology service filter results automatically. See the Value set design and management playbook for constraint authoring guidance.

decisions.question: Which language reference set determines preferred terms and search synonyms for your users?
decisions.guidance: Configure the terminology service with the correct language reference set for your clinical users. Search should match against preferred terms and acceptable synonyms from that language reference set. In any search directly connected to data entry, a single common language/dialect should be mandatory to avoid ambiguity - terms from other language reference sets (including international English) should not appear unless explicitly configured for a multilingual deployment.

decisions.question: How should search results be ordered and disambiguated?
decisions.guidance: The guide identifies five ordering factors: shortest matching term first, preferred term above synonym, the user's language preference, priority within any active ordered reference set, then frequency of prior selection. Never sort a broad, unconstrained result set alphabetically - the guide flags this as a usability and patient-safety issue; reserve alphabetical order for short, already-constrained pick-lists. Separately, decide how you will disambiguate what's left on screen: filter to one hit per concept (preferred term or closest match, not every synonym), and distinguish identical terms belonging to different concepts via hover detail or grouped headings.

decisions.question: What should happen when no matching concept is found?
decisions.guidance: Do not silently allow free-text entry as a fallback - this breaks structured data quality. Design a deliberate no-match pathway: a message explaining the concept is not in the system, guidance to try alternative terms or a broader search, and a route to request a new concept from the terminology team or SNOMED International. Widening the searchable scope (see the priority subset question below) generally reduces how often this pathway is hit at all.

decisions.question: Should you build a hand-curated priority or diagnosis subset to limit what clinicians can choose from?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED International's guidance is to avoid this. Manually enumerating a subset for data entry caps clinical expressivity, misses newly added content on each release, and works against precision-medicine and rare-disease use cases. Use ECL to define the domain boundary instead, and apply frequency-based boosting in ranking to surface commonly used concepts - this gets the same usability benefit without restricting what's available. A hand-curated subset is only justified as a temporary workaround in a legacy system that genuinely cannot load or query full SNOMED CT.

decisions.question: How will the search UX be tested with clinical users?
decisions.guidance: Test search with clinicians from the intended specialty using realistic clinical scenarios before go-live. Measure time-to-selection, error rate, and subjective satisfaction. Iterate on term coverage, ranking, and synonym configuration based on usability test findings.

steps.title: Define the concept constraint for each data entry field
steps.description: Write and test an ECL expression that defines the valid concept space for each field, and decide whether it needs a supporting reference set - for prioritisation, for exclusion (e.g. removing non-human concepts from a human medicine deployment), or because the constraint spans more than one hierarchy. Validate the resulting concept set with clinical SMEs to confirm it is clinically appropriate and correctly bounded. Apply the active-concept filter unconditionally - inactive concepts and descriptions should never be selectable in a data entry context, even as an option. Document the constraint as a named value set for use in search configuration and runtime validation. See the Value set design and management playbook for ECL authoring and testing guidance.

steps.title: Configure text-matching and language behaviour
steps.description: Beyond ECL scoping, the guide sets out how the text matching itself should behave. Support diacritic-insensitive matching (a search for "sjogren" should find "Sjögren"), prefix and substring matching, and word-order independence, since clinicians rarely type terms in the exact stored word order. If you exclude stop words to shrink the index, do not use a generic list uncritically - words like "no", "non", and "without" carry clinical meaning and must not be silently dropped from a query. Mandate a single language/dialect for any search directly connected to data entry to avoid ambiguous mixed-language results.

steps.title: Implement autocomplete search with the field constraint applied
steps.description: Integrate search into the data entry UI. The right implementation depends on whether you have access to a terminology server with full-text and ECL support - choose the option that matches your infrastructure.

steps.title: Configure ranking and disambiguate the display
steps.description: Rank matches the way clinicians read them, then disambiguate what's left on screen. Where several synonyms of the same concept match a query, filter to one hit per concept (the preferred term, or the single closest match) rather than listing every synonym separately. Where two different concepts happen to share an identical preferred term or synonym, disambiguate on hover (surface the concept's context) or group results under supertype headings. For large, less-constrained result sets, nest narrower concepts under their parent (subsumption-based display) instead of a flat list, so clinicians aren't scrolling past dozens of subtypes to find the one they want.

steps.title: Design and test the no-match pathway
steps.description: When no concept is found, display a clear message and provide a structured pathway: a link to the content request process, a fallback escalation route, or a structured free-text capture with mandatory concept request. Never allow silent free-text entry in a field designed for SNOMED CT codes. If no-match is hit often for a given field, treat that as a signal to review the field's ECL scope and synonym coverage - not as a reason to introduce a restrictive hand-picked subset.

steps.title: Offer mnemonics and personal favorites with guardrails
steps.description: Abbreviations, mnemonics, and personal or organisational favourite lists genuinely speed up entry of frequently used concepts and are worth supporting. But they only work safely alongside search that is itself easy to use - if general search is clunky, clinicians will default to whichever shortcut is closest at hand even when it maps to a less accurate concept than the encounter calls for, which can degrade data quality or, in the worst case, affect treatment. Pair any shortcut list with user education on when a full search is still needed, and monitor selected concepts for shortcut misuse.

steps.title: Conduct usability testing with clinicians and iterate
steps.description: Run usability tests with clinicians from the target specialties using realistic clinical scenarios. Measure and track time-to-selection, first-result accuracy, and free-text fallback rates. Use findings to tune synonym coverage, ECL constraints, and ranking configuration.

dependencies.text: Terminology service or database with full-text search and ECL-equivalent constraint filtering (Snowstorm is the reference implementation)
ECL-defined value sets per data entry field, optionally paired with reference sets for prioritisation or exclusion
Language reference set configured for preferred term display and synonym matching

pitfalls: Displaying FSNs (fully specified names) in search results - FSNs are technical identifiers not appropriate for clinician-facing display
Running search against all of SNOMED CT without ECL scoping - produces irrelevant results and a poor clinician experience
Allowing silent free-text fallback when no match is found - destroys structured data quality
Sorting broad, unconstrained search results alphabetically instead of by match quality and frequency - a documented usability and patient-safety issue
Hand-curating a priority or diagnosis subset as the primary way to limit clinician choice, instead of ECL scoping with frequency-based boosting - caps expressivity and misses newly added content
Ignoring synonym configuration in both directions - missing synonyms clinicians actually use, and showing every synonym of one concept as a separate hit instead of a single preferred-term result
Not testing search with clinical users before go-live - irrelevant results or missing preferred terms are only discovered in production
Using a pre-loaded static export without a refresh process on each SNOMED CT release - new concepts are silently unavailable for selection
Letting mnemonics or personal-favorite shortcuts substitute for proper search when the mapped concept doesn't actually fit the encounter
