mapping.title: Mapping SNOMED CT to/from other code systems
mapping.subtitle: Mapping SNOMED CT to and from classification, billing, and other code systems, for reporting, interoperability, or analysis
mapping.overview: SNOMED CT mapping translates SNOMED CT to other code systems - such as ICD-10, OPCS-4, or CPT - for reporting and billing, and translates other code systems into SNOMED CT for interoperability, search, or analytics. Where an official map exists, such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map, start there before building anything custom; for mapping into SNOMED CT, Snap2SNOMED is the recommended tool. Mapping to a less granular target always loses some clinical meaning, which cannot be recovered in reverse. This playbook covers building the map itself; if your goal is to migrate your own system of record onto SNOMED CT, see the Migrating to SNOMED CT playbook instead.

decisions.question: Is mapping the right solution, given the ongoing maintenance burden it creates?
decisions.guidance: Building and maintaining a map is not always the best option - especially where the source and target systems update on very different cycles (for example, a monthly-updated medication terminology against an annually revised classification). If the goal is SNOMED CT-coded data, weigh a map against capturing SNOMED CT directly at the point of documentation instead: native capture avoids the maintenance burden and is often more accurate long-term. Only commit to mapping once it is clearly the better option. If this map is part of a wider migration, see the Migrating to SNOMED CT playbook for how this decision fits into that strategy.

decisions.question: What is the purpose and direction of mapping?
decisions.guidance: Clarify whether you need SNOMED CT to a classification or billing system (such as ICD-10, OPCS-4, or CPT), another code system into SNOMED CT, or both - each direction needs different tools and quality requirements, and a unidirectional tool cannot be forced into a bidirectional map. Also confirm the source and target systems have compatible semantic domains before committing; incompatible domains undermine any map regardless of tooling. See the Analytics and reporting playbook for how SNOMED CT to ICD-10 output feeds downstream reporting.

decisions.question: Does an existing map to your target system already exist and can it be adopted or adapted?
decisions.guidance: Check whether SNOMED International, a national release centre, or another organization already maintains a map to your target system - for example, the official SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map. Load and test it first: an actively maintained existing map is almost always preferable to a custom one, which needs its own upkeep on every SNOMED CT release.

decisions.question: Has a clinical risk assessment been performed and documented for this map?
decisions.guidance: Mapping errors can propagate into clinical decisions, billing, and reporting, so quality assurance needs more than technical validation. Perform and document a formal risk assessment - risks, mitigations, and an ongoing review process - as part of the map's documentation, not as an afterthought.

decisions.question: How will ambiguous or unmappable concepts be handled?
decisions.guidance: Some source concepts have no direct target equivalent, or map to multiple targets depending on context (for example, laterality or episode of care). Record this using standard relationship types - equivalent, broader, narrower, inexact, or no match - rather than forcing an approximate one-to-one link, and define a handling policy for genuine no-match cases (expert escalation, a post-coordinated expression, or a new content request) rather than leaving it to the algorithm alone.

decisions.question: How will mapping quality be validated and maintained over time?
decisions.guidance: Map quality needs review by clinical and terminology experts, not just technical validation - dual independent mapping with an adjudicator is the gold standard; single-author mapping carries a higher risk of undetected errors. Define who samples, audits, and approves map entries, and how the map is updated on each SNOMED CT release, since unmaintained maps degrade over time. See the Governance playbook for release management guidance.

steps.title: Assess the full scope of mapping required
steps.description: Inventory all systems, workflows, and reporting destinations that need mapping output, documenting the source and target code systems, concept volume, and whether mapping needs to be real-time or batch. Identify whether an official map (such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map) covers the scope, or whether custom mapping is also needed.

steps.title: Assess and prepare source data quality
steps.description: Mapping cannot fix poor-quality source data. Review source codes and terms for ambiguous abbreviations, symbols, or free-text artifacts (for example "#", "/", "?", or shorthand comorbidity strings) before mapping begins. Agree and document interpretation rules for ambiguous entries so mappers apply them consistently, and flag entries that cannot be reliably mapped without clinical input rather than forcing a guess.

steps.title: Apply the map for your mapping direction
steps.description: The approach differs by direction. Mapping from SNOMED CT to a classification such as ICD-10: if an official map exists (such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map), load it in your terminology service as a ConceptMap resource and apply it using the FHIR $translate operation. Apply the full map algorithm including rule groups, rule priorities, and advice fields - the official map is not a simple one-to-one lookup. Mapping from another code system into SNOMED CT: use a mapping tool to create and review candidate matches. Snap2SNOMED (from SNOMED International) is a free tool that supports AI-assisted candidate generation, human review, and RF2 export for this direction; other mapping tools and manual approaches also exist. In both directions, record the map relationship type (equivalent, broader, narrower, inexact, or no match) rather than assuming all entries are exact matches.

steps.title: Validate map results against a defined QA process
steps.description: Sample mapped records and review with personnel experienced in both code systems - dual independent mapping with an adjudicator is the gold standard where risk warrants it. Check the algorithm produces expected output and that ambiguous, multi-target, or no-match cases follow the agreed policy, covering edge cases specifically. Treat AI or automation-assisted suggestions (for example, from Snap2SNOMED) as an additional mapper's input, not a substitute for this review - verify they are genuine and apply risk-based human review before accepting them.

steps.title: Implement and test in the receiving workflow
steps.description: Integrate mapped codes into the target workflow and test the end-to-end pipeline with realistic data, including edge cases such as unmapped or multi-target concepts. For reporting to a classification or billing system, confirm the output meets statutory or contractual requirements. See the Terminology service playbook for ConceptMap and $translate configuration.

steps.title: Establish map maintenance aligned to SNOMED CT releases
steps.description: Review the official map delta and any custom map entries on each SNOMED CT release, and check new concepts on either side for coverage. If SNOMED CT is the source (mapping out), resolve retired source concepts via the historical association reference sets before updating the map entry. If SNOMED CT is the target (mapping in, via Snap2SNOMED), check whether previously mapped target concepts have since been retired and update accordingly - Snap2SNOMED's versioning and review workflow supports this. See the Governance playbook for release management guidance.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with FHIR $translate operation and ConceptMap support
Official map for your target system, where one exists (for example, the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map, from RF2 release files)
Personnel with clinical, source-system, and target-terminology expertise, not clinical coders alone
Governance process for map review and update on each SNOMED CT release
Documented risk assessment and map documentation covering purpose, scope, rules, and QA process

pitfalls: Treating a rule-based extended map (such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map) as a simple lookup - these maps have rule groups, priorities, and advice fields that must all be applied to produce the correct target code
Creating a custom map when the official map already meets the need - custom maps require active maintenance on every SNOMED CT release
Not validating map output against a defined QA process - technical correctness does not guarantee clinical coding correctness

Attempting to reverse a unidirectional map - it is not intended for use in the reverse direction, and reversing it can produce nonsensical results because SNOMED CT is typically more granular than the target system

Ignoring history supplements for retired concepts - historical SNOMED CT concept IDs from older releases may be inactivated and must be resolved to current equivalents before mapping or maintaining a map
No map maintenance process - the official map is updated on each SNOMED CT release and custom maps must be reviewed against the delta to remain valid

Treating AI- or automation-assisted map suggestions (for example, from Snap2SNOMED) as reviewed output - AI should be used as an additional mapper, not a replacement for QA; check suggested concepts are genuine and apply risk-based human review

Assuming a technically well-formed map alone improves clinical utility or analytics - it only reproduces the source system's existing scope until expanded into a proper SNOMED CT value set, and mapped-data reports may not be comparable to reports built on native SNOMED CT data

migration.title: Migrating to SNOMED CT
migration.subtitle: Planning, executing, and verifying an organization-wide migration from legacy code systems and workflows onto SNOMED CT
migration.overview: Migrating an organization to SNOMED CT is more than a data conversion project - it combines data conversion, system and workflow change, terminology governance, and clinical adoption, and treating it as purely technical work is a common root cause of failed or stalled migrations. This playbook covers deciding scope and approach, choosing a terminology strategy, managing legacy data quality, executing the rollout, and verifying the migration actually succeeded rather than just declaring it complete. It assumes a map from your legacy or local code system to SNOMED CT exists or is being built alongside this work - see the Mapping playbook for the technical work of building and maintaining that map itself, including tooling, relationship types, and QA.

decisions.question: What is driving this migration, and how much scope should the first phase cover?
decisions.guidance: Migrations are typically driven by one or more of eight strategic objectives - comprehensive system integration, AI and advanced clinical decision support, standards-based interoperability, legacy data preservation, data quality and governance improvement, keeping pace with the biannual SNOMED CT release cycle, specialty content support, and clinical user adoption. Identify which of these - and which underlying driver (a regulatory deadline, clinical ambition, a greenfield build, or a multi-provider programme) - applies before scoping. Favor a contained first phase (for example, allergies alone) over pursuing all objectives simultaneously; pick three or four objectives you can measure, not all eight at once.

decisions.question: Will SNOMED CT be a reference terminology or a primary terminology, for each data domain?
decisions.guidance: Decide, per data domain, where you sit on the reference-to-primary spectrum. As a reference terminology, SNOMED CT is attached behind the scenes via interface terminology binding or batch mapping while clinicians keep using familiar terms - but coding granularity is then constrained by the map, and mapping errors produce silent coding errors, so map governance is as important as map creation. As a primary terminology, clinicians search and select SNOMED CT directly with no mapping layer, which needs more training investment but removes that constraint. Most organizations use a mixed pattern - for example, primary terminology for problem lists and allergies, reference terminology for medications, and reference terminology with downstream classification mapping for diagnoses used in billing. Document the choice per domain; see the Mapping playbook for building and maintaining the underlying map where you choose reference terminology.

decisions.question: Is this a data migration, a system migration, or both?
decisions.guidance: Data migration (converting historical records) and system migration (changing the tools and workflows clinicians use) are distinct axes with different risks and stakeholders - conflating them creates avoidable failure. Consider the four patterns this produces: full modernisation (both together), behind-the-scenes migration (data only, workflow unchanged), partial system migration (some workflows change, data conversion partial), and phased hybrid (staggered by domain or department). Also decide whether a minimum viable migration - a deliberately narrow scope delivering a defined subset of value quickly - meets your immediate need, understanding what it does not deliver, rather than treating it as a permanent end state.

decisions.question: What data migration strategy and rollout timing fits your risk tolerance and resources?
decisions.guidance: Four data migration strategies trade off upfront effort against ongoing cost: full FHIR conversion (highest upfront effort, lowest ongoing cost), API integration/facade (lower upfront effort, higher ongoing cost), strategic archiving of low-value historical data, and a hybrid approach combining these by data type and age (typically 30-50% cheaper than converting everything the same way). Separately, choose a rollout timing approach: an API-first bridge, a microservices migration, a big bang cutover with a safety net, or a phased departmental rollout - the most common pattern for larger organizations. Make these two choices together, not independently.

decisions.question: What is the risk assessment across every affected domain, and what mitigates each risk?
decisions.guidance: Assess patient safety, interoperability, data quality, operational, and compliance risk separately - each needs its own named mitigation, not a single generic sign-off. Typical mitigations include three-tier testing (technical, standards conformance, and clinical validation), parallel running of the legacy and new system for safety-critical data such as allergies before decommissioning the legacy system, and piloting in a lower-acuity department before a wider rollout.

decisions.question: How will legacy data quality and code-system diversity be handled?
decisions.guidance: Legacy data typically has systematic errors, inconsistent coding, missing clinical context, and drift across code system versions, and code systems differ in granularity, producing one-to-many and many-to-one relationships that a simple lookup cannot resolve. Standard published maps (for example, ICD-10-CM, RxNorm, or LOINC to SNOMED CT) are a starting point but need review for your specific use case before being assumed fit for purpose - see the Mapping playbook for how to assess, adapt, or build these. For large volumes, an AI-assisted mapping tool that learns from expert decisions can help, but expert clinical review of a statistically significant sample remains mandatory.

decisions.question: How will migration success be verified and demonstrated, not just declared complete?
decisions.guidance: Technical completion of a data conversion is not the same as a successful migration. Pick three or four of the strategic objectives identified at the start as measurable targets - for example, drug-allergy alert accuracy, FHIR conformance rate, data exchange success rate, SNOMED CT coverage on the problem list, or semantic search coverage - set a baseline and target for each before go-live, and measure again at go-live, 3 months, and 12 months.

steps.title: Assess objectives and scope the first phase
steps.description: Inventory candidate data domains and apply a value-effort assessment - clinical value against conversion effort - to decide what belongs in phase one versus a later phase. Select a small, measurable set of objectives (three or four, not all eight) for this phase, and document the driver behind the migration, since a regulatory deadline, a clinical ambition, a greenfield build, and a multi-provider programme each imply different scope and executive expectations.

steps.title: Decide the terminology strategy and system/data migration pattern per domain
steps.description: For each data domain in scope, decide whether SNOMED CT will be a reference terminology (bound behind the scenes) or a primary terminology (selected directly by clinicians), and whether the domain needs a full system migration, a behind-the-scenes data migration, or a minimum viable subset of both. Document these decisions domain by domain - most organizations end up with a mixed pattern rather than one approach applied uniformly.

steps.title: Choose a data migration strategy
steps.description: Select how historical data will be converted, matching your risk tolerance, timeline, and available resources.

steps.title: Choose a rollout timing approach
steps.description: Match the rollout mechanism to your organization's risk tolerance and readiness for change.

steps.title: Apply the five data-migration principles regardless of strategy
steps.description: Whichever strategy and timing you choose, apply these principles consistently: retain the original data rather than discarding it after conversion; preserve clinical context (status, verification status, category, and post-coordination where a single SNOMED CT concept cannot capture the original detail); track provenance for every converted record (source system, conversion date, process version, mapping rules applied, and validation outcome, recorded for example in a FHIR Provenance resource); validate at all three verification tiers before relying on the data clinically; and plan for ongoing change rather than treating the migration as a one-time event.

steps.title: Verify at all three tiers before relying on migrated data clinically
steps.description: Tier 1 (automated technical): FHIR structural validity, record counts, referential integrity, and performance - gates every deployment. Tier 2 (standards conformance): implementation guide conformance, SNOMED CT semantic validity, and cross-map validation. Tier 3 (clinical validation): medical appropriateness, context preservation, and decision-support correctness - this tier needs qualified clinical reviewers and cannot be automated. For safety-critical domains such as allergies, run the legacy and new system in parallel and investigate every discrepancy before decommissioning the legacy system.

steps.title: Measure success against the objectives set in phase one, and establish ongoing governance
steps.description: For each objective selected at the start, set a baseline and target and measure again at go-live, 3 months, and 12 months (example measurable targets: drug-allergy alert accuracy, FHIR conformance rate, data exchange success rate, SNOMED CT coverage on the problem list, semantic search coverage). Migration is not a one-time event: establish release management aligned to the biannual SNOMED CT release cycle (impact assessment, staging, rollback plan), ongoing value-set and data-quality monitoring, and a named terminology governance owner. See the Governance playbook for release management guidance.

dependencies.text: Named executive sponsor and terminology governance owner accountable for the migration
Core team: SNOMED CT terminology specialist, FHIR specialist, clinical subject matter experts, legacy system expert, and integration architect
Terminology server (for example, Snowstorm, or a vendor-hosted service - see SNOMED International's Terminology Services page for options) once three or more systems consume SNOMED CT-coded data
Toolchain: FHIR server, FHIR validator, a mapping tool, a testing framework, and CI/CD for staged rollout
Change management and training plan for clinical adoption, especially where SNOMED CT becomes a primary terminology

pitfalls: Treating migration as purely a data conversion project - system and workflow change, terminology governance, and clinical adoption are just as consequential, and user adoption is consistently identified as a root cause when migrations fail
Attempting all eight strategic objectives simultaneously instead of a contained, measurable first phase
Conflating data migration and system migration decisions - they carry different risk profiles and need different stakeholders in the room
Treating all legacy data as equally worth converting, instead of applying a value-effort assessment and choosing a hybrid strategy where it saves effort
Assuming a standard published map (such as ICD-10-CM, RxNorm, or LOINC to SNOMED CT) fits your use case without reviewing it in context
Decommissioning a legacy system for safety-critical data (such as allergies) without a parallel-running verification period first
Staying indefinitely at minimum viable migration scope with no plan to expand it, or treating it as a final state rather than a deliberate first step
No ongoing terminology governance after go-live - maps age and value sets drift without a named owner and a release-aligned review process

governance.title: Governance and quality assurance
governance.subtitle: Establishing governance structures for sustainable, high-quality SNOMED CT implementation
governance.overview: Governance is what separates a SNOMED CT implementation that improves over time from one that gradually degrades. Good governance defines who has authority over terminology content decisions, how changes are requested and approved, how quality is measured, and how the implementation responds to each SNOMED CT release cycle. Automated QA using ECL-based queries - for example, detecting records that use inactivated concepts - is a practical and scalable quality mechanism that should be built into the release management process from the start.

decisions.question: Who has authority over SNOMED CT terminology content decisions in your organisation?
decisions.guidance: Identify named individuals for each governance role: a clinical informaticist or Chief Clinical Information Officer for strategic decisions, a terminology lead for day-to-day curation, and specialty leads for domain-specific value set approval. Roles without named individuals produce governance vacuums where changes are made without oversight or accountability.

decisions.question: How will change requests for value sets, mappings, and concept requests be managed?
decisions.guidance: Define the full lifecycle for a change request: submission, triage, clinical review, approval, implementation, and release notification. Agree whether change requests go to a central terminology team, specialty leads, or both. Include the process for submitting new concept requests to SNOMED International via the Content Request Service. See the Value set design and management playbook for value set change management guidance.

decisions.question: How will compliance with national and SNOMED International policies be ensured?
decisions.guidance: Review your national release centre's (NRC) governance requirements and any national programme policies that apply to SNOMED CT usage. Agree how your local governance aligns with NRC processes, particularly for extension content authoring and national value set publication. See the Extensions playbook for extension-specific governance requirements.

decisions.question: How will each SNOMED CT release be assessed, tested, and deployed?
decisions.guidance: The International Edition is released monthly. National extensions follow their own schedule - typically less frequent. Each release may include concept inactivations, redefinitions, new preferred terms, and map updates. Define a release assessment process: review release notes, run regression QA queries, test consuming applications in a non-production environment, and deploy to production with a documented rollback plan.

decisions.question: What quality metrics will indicate the health of the SNOMED CT implementation?
decisions.guidance: Define measurable KPIs before go-live: coding completeness rate, preferred term adherence rate, free-text fallback rate, invalid concept usage rate, and value set coverage rate. Establish a baseline at go-live and review quarterly. ECL-based queries via the terminology service can automate most of these measurements. See the Terminology service playbook for ECL query infrastructure.

steps.title: Define and document governance roles
steps.description: Name the clinical informaticist, terminology lead, specialty leads, and governance board members. Document their responsibilities, decision-making authority, and escalation paths. Publish these roles so system teams and clinicians know who to contact for change requests and decisions.

steps.title: Establish the change control process
steps.description: Document the end-to-end process for requesting, reviewing, approving, implementing, and notifying changes to value sets, reference sets, and mappings. Include the process for submitting concept requests to SNOMED International via the Content Request Service. Processes that are too slow drive clinicians to use free text - aim for a standard change turnaround of no more than two weeks for routine requests.

steps.title: Define quality KPIs and build automated QA checks
steps.description: Define measurable quality indicators and implement automated ECL-based queries to detect quality issues: records using inactivated concept IDs, concepts outside a field's ECL constraint, or data coded at an inappropriately coarse level. Run these checks after every SNOMED CT release and review findings with the terminology lead. See the Terminology service playbook for ECL query infrastructure.

steps.title: Create a release management procedure
steps.description: Document the process for each SNOMED CT release: obtain release notes from SNOMED International or your NRC, load to a test environment, run automated QA, assess impact on value sets and maps, update content, test consuming applications, and deploy to production. The release cycle differs depending on whether you track the international release or a national extension.

steps.title: Publish and version terminology policies
steps.description: Publish the governance policy document, value set definitions, map specifications, and any local SNOMED CT usage guidelines. Version-control all policy documents so consuming teams can track changes. Make policies accessible to all system teams and clinical leads. See the Value set design and management playbook for value set versioning and publication guidance.

steps.title: Review governance effectiveness regularly
steps.description: Review KPIs quarterly and governance processes annually. Assess whether change requests are resolved within the agreed timeframe, whether QA issues are being addressed before they reach production, and whether clinicians are adopting structured coding at the expected rate. Adjust processes where evidence shows they are not working.

dependencies.text: Named governance roles with clear decision-making authority
Terminology service for ECL-based automated QA queries - see the Terminology service playbook
Documented policies, value set definitions, and change log

pitfalls: No named clinical owner for terminology content decisions - produces governance vacuums where changes are made without oversight
Governance processes so slow that change requests take months - clinicians route around the terminology system and use free text instead
No automated QA - quality issues from SNOMED CT releases (inactivated concepts, redefined preferred terms) are not detected until clinical problems arise
Ignoring SNOMED CT release notes - each release may include inactivations or preferred term changes that break downstream systems or invalidate existing value sets
Treating governance as a one-time setup activity - SNOMED CT implementations require ongoing governance investment to remain high quality
No distinction between international and national extension release cycles - missing a national extension release can leave local extension concepts unaligned with the latest international content

extensions.title: Extensions and customization
extensions.subtitle: Adding content, translations, mappings, and configuration when the international release isn't enough
extensions.overview: A SNOMED CT extension is content maintained outside the international release: new concepts, language terms, maps, or reference sets that configure SNOMED CT for a use case. Local concepts are only one of these four purposes, and often not the best one - a translation, a map, or a configuration reference set usually carries far less long-term maintenance. All extension content must follow international design principles: the MRCM concept model, hierarchy-consistent relationships, and classification. See the Multilingual, Mapping, Value set, and Governance playbooks for the other extension purposes.

decisions.question: Which of the four extension purposes applies: content, translation, mapping, or configuration?
decisions.guidance: Most extension work is not new-concept authoring. Naming the purpose first avoids defaulting to concept authoring when a reference set or a language addition would serve the need with far less ongoing maintenance.

decisions.question: What namespace will be used for new component IDs?
decisions.guidance: Every new component - concept, description, or reference set - needs an SCTID built on a registered namespace. NRCs manage a national namespace for national edition content; organisations building a private extension obtain their own namespace identifier via SNOMED International. An unregistered or shared namespace causes identifier conflicts fixable only by retiring and replacing every affected component.

decisions.question: Will the extension be distributed on its own, or packaged as an edition?
decisions.guidance: An extension is the new content itself; an edition bundles that content together with everything it depends on (the International Edition, and any national extension) into a standalone package consuming systems can load directly. Most extension producers publish as an edition rather than a bare extension, because it removes the burden of assembling the dependency chain from every consuming system. Decide this before distribution planning, since it changes what you package and version.

decisions.question: How will extension content be aligned with the international and national release?
decisions.guidance: Alignment starts at authoring, not afterwards: every new concept, relationship, or reference set member must be built against the current, active version of the international release (and national edition, if applicable) recorded in the module dependency reference set. Beyond that, each subsequent SNOMED CT international release may include new concepts that supersede extension content, or may inactivate concepts or reference set members that extension content depends on as parents, attribute values, or map targets. Define who is responsible for reviewing the release delta, retiring superseded extension content, and updating relationships. The International Edition is released monthly - build a release review process before authoring begins.

decisions.question: What classification and validation checks are required before publishing?
decisions.guidance: All new concepts must be classified using a description logic reasoner to confirm correct placement in the inferred hierarchy. Tool options vary by access: the SNOMED Authoring Platform (available to national release centres and SNOMED International members via the Managed Service) handles classification automatically; Simplex (a free tool from SNOMED International) supports translations, subsets, simple maps, and minimally-modelled concepts; and commercial SNOMED CT authoring tools also support classification and validation. Reference set content (language, map, or configuration members) is not classified but still requires RF2 structural validation. SNOMED CT's automated validation rules must pass before any content is published - these rules encode the MRCM and editorial guidance, catching modelling errors that a reasoner alone does not detect. Define the required pass rate and who approves exceptions before authoring begins.

steps.title: Prepare the technical foundation: namespace, module, and tooling
steps.description: Confirm your namespace with your NRC or SNOMED International - NRC-managed for national edition content, organisation-registered for private extensions. Create a module concept for every extension component and reference set, and record its dependencies (the International Edition, a national edition, or another extension) in the module dependency reference set, so consuming systems know what else to load. Configure your authoring tool (for example the SNOMED Authoring Platform, Simplex, or a commercial tool) with the resulting module ID, namespace, and dependencies.

steps.title: Assess the request against the extension's purpose and scope
steps.description: Confirm which purpose applies (see the decision above); translation and mapping needs go straight to the Multilingual and Mapping playbooks. For new content, search the SNOMED CT Browser across all descriptions, synonyms, and inactive terms, and submit a Content Request Service request instead of extension authoring if the concept has wider applicability. If clinical need can't wait for that decision, add it as an interim extension addition and reconcile later. Document the purpose chosen, the search performed, and why extension authoring won over an existing mechanism.

steps.title: Author content matching the chosen purpose
steps.description: Use the authoring tool from the previous step to create the content - new concepts and descriptions, or reference set members for subsets, configuration, and maps - following the Machine Readable Concept Model and Editorial Guide throughout. New concepts and descriptions carry new clinical meaning and need the most care; reference set members carry none, simply linking existing components to the extra information the use case needs.

steps.title: Review and validate in three stages
steps.description: Validation happens in three stages. During authoring: classify new concepts with the description logic reasoner - incorrect placement in the inferred hierarchy signals a modelling error - and run SNOMED CT's automated validation rules on all content, including reference sets, to catch what the reasoner doesn't (missing attributes, wrong semantic tags, a member pointing at an inactive component). After authoring: a peer reviewer checks editorial guidance and clinical usability - judgement automation can't replace. Before release: run a final validation pass over the release as a whole. Resolve all errors and warnings at every stage before promoting content further.

steps.title: Package, license, and distribute
steps.description: Package extension content as RF2 files aligned to SNOMED CT release dates, with a version date and module ID. Decide whether to distribute as a bare extension or an edition (see the decision above), and document the full dependency chain either way: international release, national edition (if applicable), then the extension. As producer, you must issue recipients an Affiliate license - which does not replace their own SNOMED CT Affiliate License for the International Release. See the Terminology service playbook for loading extension RF2 files into your terminology server and verifying counts after load.

steps.title: Maintain: process new requests and realign on each release
steps.description: Maintenance is continuous: keep triaging new change requests through the same assessment process above. Alignment starts at authoring - every component is built against the current version of its dependencies, recorded in the module dependency reference set - but each monthly international release still needs a review: evaluate the pre-production release where available, update the module dependency reference set, retire content superseded by new international content (with a historical association pointing to the replacement), update relationships or map members hit by inactivations, and reposition content under better new parents. Allow time for an alpha/beta validation pass before publishing an update. See the Governance playbook for release management guidance.

dependencies.text: SNOMED Authoring Platform or equivalent authoring tool with description logic classification
Registered SNOMED CT namespace (from your NRC or SNOMED International)
Classification (for new concepts) and automated validation (for all content) - both required before release
SNOMED CT license and NRC relationship for namespace registration

pitfalls: Assuming an extension is only for adding local concepts - a reference set, translation, or map is often the better, lower-maintenance fit
Skipping an exhaustive Browser search before authoring - the gap may already be covered by existing content or a reference set
Not submitting an international content request for a globally-applicable concept - missing SNOMED International's maintenance and keeping the local burden
Poor concept modelling - incorrect attribute-value pairs misclassify the concept and produce misleading query results
Treating validation warnings as optional - they often flag real modelling problems, not just errors
No release alignment process - content built on superseded parents, inactivated values, or retired map targets becomes invalid and breaks the terminology service
Promoting a concept internationally without retiring it in the extension - systems loading both get duplicate active concepts for the same meaning
Distributing without documenting the load order - loading the extension on the wrong edition causes classification and validation errors

multilingual.title: Multilingual implementation
multilingual.subtitle: Supporting SNOMED CT in multiple languages using language reference sets and translation tools
multilingual.overview: SNOMED CT's concept meanings are language-neutral: meaning is encoded in the concept model and defining relationships, not in text strings. Language reference sets attach preferred terms and acceptable synonyms for each language or dialect to the same underlying concept. This enables clinicians to work in their own language while the coded concept remains universally interoperable. SNOMED International and national release centres (NRCs) publish language reference sets for many languages. The SNOMED International Translation Tool supports structured translation workflows for organisations creating or maintaining translations.

decisions.question: Which language reference sets are available for your target language(s)?
decisions.guidance: Check with SNOMED International and your NRC for published language reference sets before commissioning new translations. Many languages already have reference sets maintained at national level. Using an existing national language reference set avoids duplication and benefits from NRC maintenance. See the Terminology service playbook for guidance on loading and configuring reference sets in your server.

decisions.question: What language reference set priority should the terminology service use for display and search?
decisions.guidance: Most FHIR-compliant terminology servers support language reference set priority ordering: concepts are displayed using the preferred term from the highest-priority language reference set that has an entry for that concept. If the first-priority reference set has no entry for a concept, the server falls through to the next configured reference set. Verify how your specific server handles this, configure it carefully, and test coverage gaps explicitly before go-live.

decisions.question: How will gaps in translation coverage be identified and addressed?
decisions.guidance: No language reference set covers 100% of SNOMED CT content. For concepts used in your implementation that lack preferred terms in the target language, decide whether to supplement with local translations (via the Translation Tool and a local extension - see the Extensions playbook), display the international English preferred term with a language label, or a combination. Document the coverage gap policy and apply it consistently.

decisions.question: Who has authority to approve locally added translations?
decisions.guidance: Translations carry clinical meaning and must be approved by a subject matter expert fluent in both the clinical domain and the target language. Define the approval workflow, quality criteria, and who is responsible for maintaining translations on each SNOMED CT release. See the Governance playbook for change control process guidance.

decisions.question: How will translation quality be reviewed on each SNOMED CT release?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED CT releases add new concepts that may not yet have translated preferred terms. Updated concepts may have changed FSNs that affect translation accuracy. Define a release review process: identify newly added concepts within your implementation scope, flag them for translation, and update the language reference set before the release goes to production.

steps.title: Identify available language reference sets
steps.description: Check SNOMED International's MLDS and your NRC for published language reference sets for your target language(s). Review coverage level and release cadence. Download and assess the reference set against your implementation's concept scope to understand where gaps exist before configuring the terminology service.

steps.title: Configure language reference set priority in the terminology service
steps.description: Configure the language reference set priority list in your terminology server for each deployment locale so that $lookup and concept search operations return preferred terms in the correct language. Set a fallback reference set (typically the international English language reference set) so that concepts with no preferred term in the primary language still return a display term. The approach varies by server: in Snowstorm (open source, SNOMED International), this is configured per branch. See the Terminology service playbook for guidance on your deployment.

steps.title: Identify and address translation gaps
steps.description: Run a coverage analysis: extract all SNOMED CT concept IDs used in your implementation and check whether each has a preferred term in the target language reference set. The SNOMED CT Browser shows all available descriptions for a concept by language. For concepts with gaps, choose one of two approaches.

steps.title: Use a translation tool for new or supplementary translations
steps.description: For concepts requiring local translation, a structured translation workflow tool supports source term display, translation entry, review, approval, and RF2 export. The SNOMED International Translation Tool is one such tool designed for this purpose. The exported RF2 description and language reference set files are then loaded into a terminology server as a local extension on top of the national edition. For new translated descriptions added to a local extension, also see the Extensions playbook.

steps.title: Test with native-language clinical users
steps.description: Test term display and search with clinicians working in each target language. Verify that preferred terms are clinically natural and that search returns the expected results using language-specific clinical terminology. Confirm that fallback terms are visually distinguishable from natively translated terms. Correct any terms that are technically accurate but clinically unfamiliar.

steps.title: Establish translation governance and release review cycle
steps.description: Define who approves translations, the quality review criteria, and the process for reviewing new and changed concepts on each SNOMED CT release. Align translation release timing with the SNOMED CT release cycle so consuming systems receive updated language reference sets before corresponding SNOMED CT content goes to production. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

dependencies.text: Terminology service (Snowstorm) with language reference set priority configuration
National or international language reference sets in RF2 format
Clinical SMEs fluent in the clinical domain and target language for translation review
Governance process for translation approval and release review

pitfalls: Displaying FSNs (in English) to non-English-speaking clinicians - always configure preferred terms from the appropriate language reference set
Assuming translation coverage is complete - all language reference sets have gaps, particularly for recently added concepts
No fallback language reference set configured in the terminology service - concepts with no preferred term in the primary language return no display text at all
Locally added translations without governance - unapproved terms may introduce clinical meaning errors that are hard to detect
Not loading translated descriptions as a proper RF2 extension - ad hoc term overrides in application code bypass the terminology service and break interoperability
No release review process - new concepts added in SNOMED CT releases go without translation and appear in English (or without display text) in clinical systems
